hook_patterns: Start with [sourced valuation scenario], identify its largest assumption, and preview the calculation that would test it.
Place [reported operating result] beside [verified price reaction], then ask which expectation could explain the difference.
Compare [two companies] using the same [financial metric]; preview why the lower share price need not mean the cheaper business.

Put [verified insider purchase] beside [existing ownership or compensation] before discussing its significance. Optional original analogy hypothesis: measure the purchase against the wallet, not just the receipt.
packaging_notes: AI selection and valuation framing has repeated strong signals: 9.6x and 8.6x baseline on one channel, plus 6.1x on another. The first two share a channel and overlapping baselines, so they are not independent replications. This supports testing specific comparisons, not claiming stocks are bargains.

Named authorities and quantified scenarios accompany strong signals, including SpaceX at 86.0x, a tech/AI analyst discussion at 37.1x, and Tesla at 24.4x. Treat source-title forecasts as unverified claims; transfer the assumption-testing structure, not guaranteed upside or borrowed authority.

No duration sweet spot is established. Strong AI examples include 54–60 seconds, 5:41 and 15:56; strong Tesla/SpaceX examples run 9:29–15:45. Analyze short-duration and longer formats separately; the <=180-second bucket does not establish Shorts distribution.

Result-versus-price contradictions and insider-purchase context are exploratory: APLD is emerging at 7.9x with 1,832 views; Celsius at 5.4x with 2,002; SoFi at 2.9x with 1,105. Nike remains emerging despite 79.5x because its 83,300 subscribers exceed the strong-tier limit. Verify the underlying events before using these frames.

These are packaging associations from September 10–October 9 uploads, not proof of what caused performance this week. Baselines are not equal-age comparisons; no thumbnails, transcripts or retention curves were supplied. All opening shapes and humor are hypotheses. Reject panic, urgency and unsupported return promises; use numbers for comparisons and explicit scenarios.
market_patterns.title: outlier pattern extraction

winning_patterns: Among Shorts, company or ticker + quantified move + named catalyst is a promising structure: three examples retained 88.8–99.8% APV with hook-window readings of 1.194–1.357. Frame the opening around the move and its explanation; actual opening scripts were not supplied.

For insider Shorts, executive role + transaction direction + dollar amount provides a compact factual frame. The purchase example held 82.7% APV and a 1.177 hook reading, while one sale example held 77.7% and 1.185. Treat this as a format to test, not evidence that purchases outperform sales.
losing_patterns: In the two long videos, transaction summaries carrying dollar amounts plus filing or transaction-count detail coincided with 38.1–44.9% APV and 0.633–0.661 hook readings. Avoid assuming administrative detail is a strong opening payoff; this sample cannot separate packaging from duration effects.

Within Shorts, a generic upward-move verb plus a disclosure catalyst, without a quantified move, appeared in the weakest APV example at 68.0%, with a 1.053 hook reading. Avoid relying on excitement language alone, but treat this single example as a weak signal rather than a rule.
notes: The sample contains only 10 Shorts and two long videos, with 41–726 views each. Title structures correlate with performance here; opening scripts, impressions and distribution evidence are absent.

Market-close Shorts span 68.0–99.8% APV; insider Shorts span 69.9–156.1%. The 156.1% insider result had only 88 views and 24 engaged views, so replay-influenced retention is not proof of broad demand or franchise superiority.

Keep Shorts and long-video baselines separate. APV measures viewing depth, not swipe-away or feed conversion; supplied hook readings above 1 should not be interpreted as percentages of unique viewers retained.
